newsitem.title: USA: Calif. to spend $500-mln-plus on classrooms - report.
newsitem.headline: Calif. to spend $500-mln-plus on classrooms - report.

text.p: At least $500 million will be spent in California in the current year to provide new classrooms under the state's class size reduction program, according to a report released on Wednesday.

California's Legislative Analyst estimated that total statewide expenditures for facilities for the class size reduction program would be at least $500 million in the current year, or about $28,000 per new classroom on average.
The state legislature and the governor created the class size reduction program as part of the 1996-1997 budget.

The program is intended to reduce average class sizes from 28.6 students to no more than 20 students in up to three grades. The governor's 1997-1998 budget proposes expansion of the class size reduction (CSR) program to four grades.

Even though the program's target is 20 students, the Legislative Analyst said districts have been maintaining CSR classes at a ratio of 19 students to one teacher to be sure of remaining under the cap of 20 students to one teacher.
"This increases per-pupil CSR costs by as much as 21 percent," the Legislative Analyst said in its report.

Future facility costs for the class size reduction program will depend on whether school districts average 19 or 20 students per class, and on whether the governor's expansion proposal is adopted, the Legislative Analyst said.
If districts maintain the 19 student average, the Legislative Analyst said another $600 million may be needed for facilities to fully implement the program in three grades.
These additional facility costs would drop to about $250 million for average class sizes of 20 in the three grades, the Legislative Analyst said.

The Legislative Analyst said an additional $500 million would be needed to implement the class size reduction program in four grades as proposed by the governor, assuming average class sizes of 20 students.
As part of its report, the Legislative Analyst issued a set of recommendations that would adjust the class size reduction program to ease the burden on school districts.

The Legislative Analyst recommended that the state legislature redefine the student-to-teacher cap to require a 20-to-1 average ratio in each district, while allowing individual classes to have up to 22 students.

Citing the high cost of new facilities and shortage of qualified teachers, the Legislative Analyst also recommended that the legislature delay expansion of the class size reduction program to a fourth grade and provide additional funds to districts.
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst provides fiscal and policy advice to the state legislature.
